title: HTML Text and Headings
description: Learn how to structure readable, meaningful webpage content using headings, paragraphs, emphasis and lists.

pages.title: Welcome Back! Let's Build Better Webpages
pages.content: Hi there! Welcome back to Code Academy! 👋 You are now starting Lesson 2 of your HTML journey. In our first lesson, you discovered what HTML is and learned the basic structure of an HTML document. Today, we're going to make that structure useful. Think about a website you visit every day. You don't see one giant block of text. You see a main heading, smaller headings, paragraphs, important words and lists. Those things help people understand a webpage quickly. Today, you're going to learn how to create those structures yourself. And remember our bigger goal: we're not learning HTML just to memorize tags. We're learning it so that one day you can open your editor and confidently build a real website.
pages.voice: Hi there! Welcome back to Code Academy! You are now starting Lesson 2 of your HTML journey. In our first lesson, you discovered what HTML is and learned the basic structure of an HTML document. Today, we're going to make that structure useful. We're going to learn how professional webpages organize their written content. So, are you ready? Let's begin!

pages.title: HTML Gives Your Content Meaning
pages.content: Before we learn individual elements, let's understand one very important idea. HTML is not simply a tool for making text look big, small, bold or colorful. HTML describes what your content means and how your document is organized. Imagine handing a book to someone with no chapter titles, no paragraphs and no organization. The information might still exist, but understanding it would be much harder. HTML gives webpages that organization. CSS will later help us control the visual design. JavaScript will later help us add behavior. For now, HTML is our structure.
pages.voice: Before we learn individual elements, I want you to understand one very important idea. HTML is not simply a tool for making text look big, small, bold or colorful. HTML describes what your content means and how your document is organized. CSS will later control the design, and JavaScript will later add behavior. But HTML gives the webpage its structure.

Because it identifies the content as the main heading
interaction.explanation: Exactly! HTML should communicate the meaning and structure of your content. Its appearance can later be controlled with CSS.

pages.title: Understanding h1 to h6
pages.content: HTML provides six heading levels: h1, h2, h3, h4, h5 and h6. Think of them as levels in a document. The h1 is normally the highest-level heading. An h2 can introduce a major section under that heading. An h3 can introduce a subsection inside the h2 section. This hierarchy helps both humans and software understand your document. Don't choose a heading just because you like its visual size. Choose it because it makes sense in the structure of your content.
pages.voice: HTML provides six heading levels: h1, h2, h3, h4, h5 and h6. Think of them as levels in an organized document. H1 is the highest level, then H2, then H3, continuing down to H6. Here's the important part: don't choose a heading just because of how large it looks. Choose it based on the structure and importance of your content.

pages.title: Paragraphs: Give Your Website a Voice
pages.content: A heading introduces a topic, but paragraphs explain that topic. The p element is used for normal paragraphs. A professional webpage will usually contain many paragraphs, each communicating a particular idea. Avoid putting an entire page into one enormous paragraph. Break your information into logical pieces so your users can understand it easily. This is especially important when you eventually build business websites, portfolios, social-media-style interfaces and other real projects.
pages.voice: A heading introduces a topic, but paragraphs explain that topic. The P element is used for normal paragraphs. A professional webpage can contain many paragraphs, with each paragraph communicating a particular idea. Let's see how that works.

pages.title: Strong and Emphasized Text
pages.content: Sometimes a normal paragraph is not enough. You may want to communicate that a particular word or phrase is especially important. HTML provides the strong element for strong importance and the em element for emphasis. These elements are useful because they communicate meaning. They are not simply decoration. Later, CSS can change their visual appearance without changing the underlying meaning of the HTML.
pages.voice: Sometimes a normal paragraph isn't enough. You may want to communicate that a particular word or phrase is especially important. HTML gives us the strong element for strong importance and the em element for emphasis. Let's look at both.

pages.title: Lists: Organize Information
pages.content: Now we're going to add another powerful structure: lists. Imagine you are creating a website that shows the programming languages you know. You could place them all inside a paragraph, but that would not be very clear. A list would be much better. HTML gives us unordered lists with ul and ordered lists with ol. Each item inside either list is created with li. Use an unordered list when the order doesn't matter. Use an ordered list when the sequence matters.

pages.title: Put Everything Together
pages.content: You've now learned headings, paragraphs, strong importance, emphasis and lists. Let's combine them into one small but realistic webpage. This is how you should think as a developer. Individual HTML elements are building blocks. Your job is to combine those blocks into a meaningful document. Don't just copy this example. Study the structure and ask yourself what you would change if this were your own website.
pages.voice: You've learned several important building blocks. Now let's combine them into one realistic webpage. This is how web development works. You learn individual pieces, understand what they do, and then combine them to create something useful. Watch carefully.
